claims.text: A silicide coating can be applied to a high-entropy alloy by pack cementation.
The pack-cemented coating forms an outer MSi2 layer and an inner MSi layer.
The untreated alloy is nanocrystalline and has high hardness and strength.
The untreated alloy suffers from surface oxidation and inadequate tribological performance, particularly at elevated temperature.
Pack cementation produces a dense, adherent silicide bilayer.
The silicide bilayer minimizes uncontrolled oxidation.
At elevated temperatures, the coating promotes controlled tribo-oxidation that forms lubricious oxides such as (Zr,Hf)O2.
The tribo-formed oxides seal cracks and make the interface self-healing.
The silicide layer acts as a barrier to rapid oxidation and thereby reduces abrasive wear.
An in-situ lubricious oxide film reduces mechanical interlocking and adhesive wear.
The coating will reduce both friction and wear from room temperature to at least 300 °C, with possible effectiveness at higher temperatures.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the coating may reduce coefficient of friction by 30–50%.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the coating may reduce wear rate by one to two orders of magnitude.
Untreated high-entropy-alloy surfaces have higher friction because of uncontrolled oxide formation and surface degradation.
Untreated high-entropy-alloy surfaces wear faster than silicide-coated surfaces under sliding.
Thermal-expansion mismatch can crack the coating and reduce its effectiveness.
Poor coating uniformity or adhesion can reduce the intervention's effectiveness.
Silicide coatings have demonstrated dramatic oxidation-resistance improvements in related refractory high-entropy alloys.
The cited refractory HfNbTaTiZr alloy was silicide-coated by pack cementation at 950 °C for 24 hours.
The magnitude of the tribological improvement depends on alloy composition and test conditions.
